title: Before You Say “I Love You”… Make Sure You Know What Love Actually Is
paragraphs:
Before You Say “I Love You”… Make Sure You Know What Love Actually Is
The Three Words That Build Heaven—or Break Hearts Forever
There are few moments in life more powerful than looking into someone's eyes and saying, "I love you."
Three simple words.

Yet those three words have started families, healed broken souls, inspired lifelong faithfulness, ignited wars of jealousy, shattered innocent hearts, justified sin, and even been spoken moments before betrayal.
Almost everyone longs to hear them.
Almost everyone longs to say them.
But what if the greatest danger isn't failing to find someone who loves you?
What if the greatest danger is believing you understand love when you've never met the One who invented it?
Before you say, "I love you," pause.
Because heaven defines love very differently than our culture does.
The world says love is a feeling.
God says love is a covenant.
The world says, "Follow your heart."
Scripture says:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9, ESV)

The Hebrew word translated "heart" is לֵב (lēḇ). It refers not merely to emotion but to the entire inner person—our thoughts, desires, intentions, and will. Jeremiah warns that the fallen human heart is unreliable when separated from God. Left to itself, it deceives us. Feelings are real, but they are not always truthful guides.
How many relationships began because two people followed their hearts, only to discover later that passion without truth eventually becomes pain?
Our generation has confused chemistry with compatibility.
Attraction with commitment.
Emotion with obedience.
Lust with love.
But Jesus never called us to follow feelings.
He called us to follow Him.
When Jesus restored Peter after Peter denied Him three times, the conversation became one of the most profound discussions about love in all of Scripture.
Jesus asked:
Σίμων Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με;
Simōn Iōannou, agapas me?
"Simon, son of John, do you love Me?" (John 21:15)
The Greek verb ἀγαπάω (agapaō) describes self-giving, sacrificial love—a love that seeks another's good regardless of personal cost.
Peter answered:
Κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε.
Kyrie, sy oidas hoti philō se.
"Lord, You know that I love You."

Peter used φιλέω (phileō), often expressing deep affection or brotherly love. Much has been written about the distinction between these terms, and while scholars debate how strongly John intends the nuance here, the scene unmistakably emphasizes that genuine love for Christ is demonstrated through faithful obedience and shepherding His people, not merely through emotional declarations.
Jesus replied:
"Feed My sheep."
Notice what Jesus did not ask.
He did not ask Peter how emotional he felt.
He did not ask how romantic his affection was.
He asked whether Peter loved Him enough to obey Him.
Biblical love always moves toward faithful action.
The Apostle John later writes:
Love is not first defined by butterflies.
Love is defined by a cross.
Long before you ever whispered "I love you" to another person...
Jesus demonstrated it first.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Notice the timing.
Not after we became holy.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we deserved forgiveness.
While we were still sinners.
That is the Gospel.
Not humanity climbing toward God.
God descending toward humanity.
The Apostle Paul gives perhaps the most quoted description of love:
"Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way..." (1 Corinthians 13:4–5)

The Greek word for love throughout this passage is ἀγάπη (agapē)—the same family of words describing self-giving love. It is steadfast, patient, enduring, and rooted in the character of God rather than in changing emotions.
Now ask yourself something uncomfortable.
Is that the kind of love you're preparing to offer?
Or are you hoping someone else will satisfy needs that only Christ can truly fulfill?
Many relationships collapse because two empty people expect each other to become gods.
Only Jesus can carry that weight.
Your future spouse was never meant to become your savior.
Your boyfriend cannot redeem your soul.
Your girlfriend cannot heal every wound.
Your husband cannot replace Christ.
Your wife cannot become your ultimate hope.
Only Jesus bears that title.
Sometimes people say "I love you" when what they really mean is:
"I need you."
"I don't want to be alone."
"I like how you make me feel."
"I fear losing you."
Those feelings are understandable, but they are not the same as biblical love.
Real love asks a different question:
"How can I glorify God by serving you?"
Everything changes when Christ becomes the center.
The greatest love story in history was never Romeo and Juliet.
It was the Holy God pursuing rebellious sinners through the life, death, and resurrection of His Son.
Every Christian marriage, every faithful friendship, every act of forgiveness, every restored family becomes a small reflection of that greater story.
This is why Scripture teaches:
"We love because He first loved us." (1 John 4:19)
The initiative belongs to God.
The source belongs to God.
The power belongs to God.
And therefore, the glory belongs to God.
Perhaps you have already said "I love you" to someone who eventually walked away.
Maybe your heart still carries scars from promises that dissolved into silence.
Perhaps you have been betrayed.
Abandoned.
Cheated on.
Manipulated.
Maybe you are ashamed because you gave your heart away too quickly, or perhaps you were the one who wounded someone else.
The Gospel does not deny those wounds.
It speaks directly into them.
Jesus Himself was betrayed with a kiss.
Denied by a close friend.
Rejected by many He came to save.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Yet from the cross He prayed:
"Father, forgive them..." (Luke 23:34)
This is why our story is always From Scandal to Grace.
Human failure is never the final chapter when Christ is the Author.
Repentance is not the end of your story.
It is often where the real story begins.
If today you are waiting for someone to love you, seek Christ first.
If you are dating, pursue holiness before romance.
If you are engaged, build your relationship on truth before emotion.
If you are married, remember that covenant love is strengthened daily through forgiveness, humility, repentance, and faithful service.
And if your heart is broken, know this:
Jesus specializes in rewriting broken stories.
He has never run out of grace.
Not once.

If this message stirred something deep within you, don't keep it to yourself. Sometimes one shared message becomes the conversation God uses to rescue a heart, restore a relationship, or point someone to Christ.
Truth is worth revisiting.

Your support enables us to continue producing biblically faithful articles, devotionals, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered content that points people to Jesus Christ rather than to ourselves.
One decision rooted in Christ can rewrite generations.
